newsitem.title: USA: Unions from rival US airlines to brief each other.
newsitem.headline: Unions from rival US airlines to brief each other.

text.p: Union officials from several major U.S. airlines will meet Sunday to update each other on the status of labor talks at their respective carriers.
Air Line Pilots Association (ALPA) officials at USAir Group Inc, Northwest Airlines Corp, UAL Corp's United Airlines, Delta Air Lines Inc and Trans World Airlines Inc are to attend the briefing.

At the "negotiating briefing," leaders of the pilots' unions will "share data relating to negotiations recently concluded or currently underway at those carriers," according to a union information hotline for pilots at USAir.
Officials from the Allied Pilots Association (APA), which represent AMR Corp's American Airlines pilots, also have been invited to speak.
American's pilots enter final negotiations with management on Monday in Washington. A strike could happen as early as Feb 15 if no settlement is reached.

American executives and union officials met on Thursday to outline their positions, but union representatives said little progress was made during the informational briefing. American has campaigned for the White House to appoint an arbitrator to settle the dispute and prevent a costly strike, sources said.
Union representatives said they would object to arbitration -- a process that could drag on for several years. The pilots said they would prefer a negotiated settlement but are willing to strike.

Labor groups throughout the airline industry are closely montoring the stalemate at American Airlines. Analysts said a strike would give strength to unions at rival carriers who seek a larger share of the industry's recent prosperity.
New contracts at American, for example, could set the standard for other labor groups' demands, analysts said.
One industry expert said this weekend's briefing suggests unions are taking a tougher, more united approach.

Labor woes have grown at several carriers: USAir has asked its pilots to accept wage cuts of up to 12 percent at a time when most union are seeking raises. United's pilots recently rejected a mid-term wage pact that offered 10 percent pay increases over four years.
Northwest and its union are haggling about whether workers should get raises on top of a recent "snap back" to 1993 wage levels, when employees took pay cuts.
Continental Airlines Inc will begin wage negotiations with its pilots in April. The pilots recently warned they were seeking hefty wage increases.
